narrativeReportMd:
# dateTime R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
The R6 ballot `dateTime` primitive keeps the same artifact identity and element shape, but its local primitive regex changed in two material ways. One is a hard R4-to-R6 validation break for dateTimes with more than 9 fractional-second digits. The other widens the R6 regex so full date-times without an offset, and even values ending in a bare `+` or `-`, can match the computable regex; those values are not R4-representable and conflict with the R6 prose that still says a UTC offset SHALL be populated when hours and minutes are specified.

## Scope
The analysis covers the `dateTime` StructureDefinition in the R4 and R6 core packages, package metadata, package indexes, and nearby primitive/base definitions needed to separate local changes from inherited hierarchy changes. The global move of primitive datatypes under `PrimitiveType` is out of scope for `dateTime` findings.

## Main migration themes
The main migration concern is primitive lexical validation. Existing R4 data with very high precision fractional seconds can fail R6 regex validation. In the reverse direction, R6 systems that trust the ballot regex can produce offset-less or malformed-offset dateTimes that R4 parsers and validators reject.

## Highest-impact findings
`dateTime:VALUE_CONSTRAINT:dateTime.value:fractional-precision-9` is the direct hard instance-breaking change. `dateTime:VALUE_CONSTRAINT:dateTime.value:offset-optionality` is the higher-risk cross-version and conformance issue because it affects timezone/offset semantics for a widely used primitive.

## Findings requiring human review
The offset finding requires human review because the R6 computable regex and R6 prose are not aligned in the supplied StructureDefinition.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The fractional-second limit may be intended to align with nanosecond precision, but it could have been introduced with a warning or compatibility rule rather than rejecting old data. The offset widening appears avoidable if unintended: keeping the R4 mandatory-offset group while changing wording from time zone to UTC offset would have preserved R4 compatibility.

## Follow-up analysis
PrimitiveType/DataType hierarchy changes and inherited Element constraint metadata should be reviewed in their own base-artifact reports.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: The local `dateTime` element model is stable, but the primitive regex is not. R4 values with more than 9 fractional-second digits become invalid in R6, and the R6 regex appears to accept offset-less or malformed-offset full date-times that R4 cannot represent. The main uncertainty is whether the offset widening is intentional or a ballot regex defect.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should focus on lexical dateTime validation and parser behavior. R4-to-R6 migrations need to detect and normalize fractional seconds beyond 9 digits. R6-to-R4 exchange should reject or repair full date-times lacking a real UTC offset, even if a regex-driven R6 validator accepts them.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for the computable StructureDefinition deltas because the regex strings and element metadata are present in both packages. Confidence is lower on the intended semantics of the offset change because the R6 prose still requires a UTC offset while the R6 regex makes the offset group optional and permits a bare sign.

findings.title: dateTime fractional seconds are capped at 9 digits in the R6 regex

oldState.summary: The R4 regex allowed one or more fractional-second digits with no explicit upper bound.
oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 `dateTime` with a complete time and UTC offset could carry an arbitrary-length fractional second component according to the regex extension.

newState.summary: The R6 regex allows only 1 to 9 fractional-second digits.
newState.narrativeMd: The R6 `dateTime` regex caps the fractional second component at 9 digits, effectively limiting precision to nanoseconds for lexical validation.

facts.note: The type stayed the same; only the regex extension narrowed.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The finding compares the same `dateTime.value` ElementDefinition id and path in both StructureDefinitions.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break: an R4-valid primitive value such as `2020-05-20T12:34:56.1234567890Z` matches the R4 regex but not the R6 regex. Runtime risk is medium because many implementations already store dateTimes at millisecond, microsecond, or nanosecond precision, but systems preserving arbitrary precision strings can fail validation or silently truncate.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is mainly data fidelity and interoperability. Clinical/business impact is low unless downstream workflows depend on sub-nanosecond precision or exact lexical preservation.

justification.inferredGoal: Constrain dateTime precision to a widely implemented and interoperable maximum, likely nanosecond precision.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep accepting fractions longer than 9 digits in the base regex, but add warnings and canonicalization guidance to normalize to 9 digits.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: unbounded fractional seconds are hard for many parsers, databases, and generated models to handle uniformly, while a 9-digit cap aligns with common nanosecond precision. A less-breaking path exists, but it would not fully meet a base-datatype goal of bounded lexical precision. Given the rarity of sub-nanosecond dateTime values and the material validator/interoperability tradeoff of leaving them valid, the break is probably justified even though no official rationale was available in the local inputs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would retain the R4 acceptance of arbitrary-length fractional seconds and add conformance text, a best-practice warning, or profile guidance recommending rounding, truncation, or rejection above 9 digits. That would preserve all old R4 instances, but it is only a partial alternative because arbitrary-precision values would remain valid in the base R6 datatype and implementations could not rely on a hard nanosecond maximum without extra policy.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves rare high-precision R4 values, but leaves base R6 validators unable to enforce a uniform nanosecond ceiling and keeps arbitrary-precision parser burden.

evidence.detail: R4 fractional seconds use an unbounded one-or-more digit pattern.
R6 fractional seconds use a 1-to-9 digit pattern.

examples.examplesMd: The example uses a representative dateTime-valued resource element rather than a complete resource. The migration example truncates to 9 digits; systems should decide whether truncation, rounding, or rejection is appropriate for their precision policy.

findings.narrativeMd: `dateTime.value` changed from accepting any number of fractional-second digits to accepting at most 9. This is a hard lexical validation change for existing R4 payloads that preserved more than nanosecond precision as strings. The element name, cardinality, and FHIRPath type are unchanged, so the break is concentrated in primitive regex validation and parser/codegen precision handling.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid dateTime with 10 or more fractional digits can become invalid in R6. This does not create an R6-to-R4 representability problem because any R6 value satisfying the 9-digit limit also satisfies R4's fractional-second portion, assuming the rest of the value is R4-compatible.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Scan dateTime-valued elements for fractional seconds longer than 9 digits before R6 validation. Choose a precision policy and apply it consistently: reject, truncate, or round. If exact lexical preservation is required, store the original value in an extension or audit trail because normalized R6 dateTime strings cannot carry the extra digits.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been less disruptive by accepting the R4 lexical space and adding guidance or warnings for values beyond 9 digits. The tradeoff is that validators would not be able to rely on a bounded precision without additional policy.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 accepts a full dateTime with any positive number of fractional-second digits, while the R6 regex accepts only 1 through 9 digits. That means an exact R4 string such as `2020-05-20T12:34:56.1234567890Z` can fail R6 primitive validation. The affected artifact is a normative, widely reused primitive, so a hard lexical narrowing deserves a real justification. On balance, the break looks proportionate because sub-nanosecond lexical precision is uncommon in FHIR exchange, a 9-digit cap aligns with broadly implementable nanosecond precision, and leaving the base datatype unbounded would keep parser, database, and SDK precision burdens in place. Implementers still need an explicit migration policy for rare over-precision values, but the change does not appear to require redesign.
keyEvidence: Regex spot-check: `2020-05-20T12:34:56.1234567890Z` full-matches R4 and not R6; the 9-digit variant matches both.
R4 maturity context supplied as normative; local r4-maturity map also marks dateTime standardsStatus normative.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative status raises the compatibility bar for any old-valid/new-invalid primitive change. It did not change the mechanism, but it made me require a proportionate interoperability rationale; the rarity and bounded-precision benefit keep the concern below Revisit.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances with more than 9 fractional-second digits in a dateTime value become invalid under the R6 regex, and exact lexical preservation may require rejection, rounding, truncation, or separate archival storage.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have retained the unbounded R4 fractional-second regex and added warning-level guidance or canonicalization advice above 9 digits. That would preserve all R4 strings, but it would not give base R6 validators or generated libraries a hard, uniform maximum precision.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing medium-impact, hard-instance-break assessment and the partial less-breaking alternative judgment; the fresh review gives more weight to normative stability but reaches the same practical conclusion that the break is probably proportionate.

findings.title: R6 dateTime regex appears to allow missing or incomplete UTC offsets for full date-times

oldState.summary: The R4 regex required a timezone/offset suffix when a time component was present.

valueLimits.regex: Full date-times required `(Z|(\+|-)... )` after seconds/fractional seconds.

semanticText.definition: If hours and minutes are specified, a time zone SHALL be populated.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, a value with a time component such as `2020-05-20T12:34:56` did not match the regex unless it ended in `Z` or a numeric offset.

newState.summary: The R6 regex makes the UTC offset group optional and also makes the numeric offset after a plus/minus sign optional.

valueLimits.regex: Full date-times use `(Z|(\+|-)((... )|14:00)?)?`, so the whole suffix and the numeric part after `+`/`-` are optional.

semanticText.definition: If hours and minutes are specified, a UTC offset SHALL be populated.
semanticText.comment: UTC offset is allowed for dates and partial dates

newState.narrativeMd: The R6 prose still says a UTC offset SHALL be populated when hours and minutes are specified, but the computable regex matches examples without an offset and examples with only a trailing `+` or `-`.

facts.note: The prose was clarified, but the R6 regex widened in the opposite direction.

facts.newValue: UTC offset is allowed for dates and partial dates
facts.note: This R6 comment is not reflected in the regex, which still does not permit an offset on date-only or partial-date forms.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same `dateTime.value` regex extension is compared in both versions. Test values `2020-05-20T12:34:56`, `2020-05-20T12:34:56+`, and `2020-05-20T12:34:56-` do not match R4 but do match the R6 regex.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 break because it widens the regex. It is high impact for R6-to-R4 exchange and runtime validation because regex-driven R6 systems can accept or emit dateTimes that R4 validators reject. Offset-less local date-times also create semantic ambiguity about the instant represented, and sign-only offsets are likely malformed even within R6.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: For clinical and operational timestamps, losing or omitting the offset can shift interpretation across time zones. The sign-only case is probably rare, but accepting it would be a data quality defect.

justification.inferredGoal: Possibly clarify terminology from time zone to UTC offset, or intentionally permit local date-times; the supplied inputs do not confirm the intent.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable to R4-to-R6 break avoidance: this offset change widens the lexical space and does not make R4-valid full dateTimes invalid in R6.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 prose still says a UTC offset SHALL be populated when hours and minutes are specified, while the R6 regex appears to accept missing offsets and even a bare trailing sign. That internal inconsistency makes the widened regex not clearly justified. However, this finding is a reverse-direction representability and runtime-conformance risk rather than an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 base-design break, so the backward-compatible alternative classification is not applicable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed for this finding because the offset widening preserves the relevant R4-valid full dateTime strings. A clearer R6 design would keep the R4 mandatory offset group for full date-times while changing the wording from time zone to UTC offset, or explicitly add local date-time support with unambiguous conformance rules. Those choices would reduce R6-to-R4 surprises, but they are not migration guidance, backport extensions, or backwards-compatible alternatives to an R4-to-R6 break.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeping mandatory offsets would improve cross-version safety, but would limit any intended support for local full date-times; that is a conformance design choice, not a less-breaking R4-to-R6 alternative.

evidence.detail: R4 prose requires a time zone when hours and minutes are specified.
evidence.quote: If hours and minutes are specified, a time zone SHALL be populated.

evidence.detail: R4 regex makes the timezone/offset suffix mandatory inside the time component.
R6 prose still requires a UTC offset when hours and minutes are specified.
evidence.quote: If hours and minutes are specified, a UTC offset SHALL be populated.

evidence.detail: R6 regex makes the entire offset suffix optional and makes the numeric part after a sign optional.
R6 adds a comment about UTC offsets on dates and partial dates, but the supplied regex does not permit those forms without a time component.
evidence.quote: UTC offset is allowed for dates and partial dates

examples.examplesMd: The examples are representative dateTime-valued element fragments. They match the R6 regex observed in the StructureDefinition but do not match the R4 regex. The sign-only example should be treated as malformed unless the ballot text explicitly confirms otherwise.

findings.narrativeMd: The R6 `dateTime.value` regex widens the lexical space for full date-times by making the UTC offset optional. It also appears to permit a trailing `+` or `-` without offset digits. This is surprising because both R4 and the R6 definition text say that an offset/time zone is required when a time is present. Systems that generate validators or parsers directly from the regex can therefore accept R6 strings that are not safe for R4 exchange and may not be semantically well-defined.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid instances do not become invalid because of this specific widening. The compatibility problem is the reverse: R6 regex-valid values such as `2020-05-20T12:34:56` and `2020-05-20T12:34:56+` are not R4-valid. If an R6 validator enforces the prose SHALL separately, offset-less values may still be rejected, but that would mean R6 regex-only and full-conformance validation disagree.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not rely only on the R6 regex for cross-version exchange. For R6-to-R4 conversion, require full date-times to end in `Z` or a complete numeric offset before emitting R4. Reject sign-only offsets as malformed. Add regression tests for offset-less, `Z`, numeric-offset, and sign-only cases, and confirm the behavior of the specific R6 validator used in production.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: If the regex widening was accidental, the backward-compatible fix is straightforward: keep the R4 mandatory offset suffix while updating prose from `time zone` to `UTC offset`. If the widening was intentional to support local times, it should be expressed explicitly and accompanied by migration guidance because R4 has no equivalent lexical representation for a full date-time without an offset.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review should determine whether the R6 ballot regex intentionally permits offset-less full date-times and sign-only offsets. The current StructureDefinition evidence is internally inconsistent.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The R6 regex widens full dateTime lexical acceptance so that values with no UTC offset, and even values ending in only `+` or `-`, can match. That does not reject old R4 data, but it creates a central cross-version and conformance hazard: the R6 definition text still says a UTC offset SHALL be populated when hours and minutes are specified, while regex-driven validators or SDKs could accept values that R4 rejects and that are ambiguous or malformed for timestamp exchange. Because dateTime is normative and appears throughout clinical and operational resources, this inconsistency should be resolved in the base definition rather than left to implementers.
keyEvidence: R4 dateTime definition says a time zone SHALL be populated when hours and minutes are specified, and the R4 regex requires `Z` or a numeric offset after the time.
R6 dateTime definition says a UTC offset SHALL be populated when hours and minutes are specified.
R6 dateTime.value regex uses an optional offset suffix and makes the numeric portion after `+` or `-` optional.
Local R6 root comment says UTC offset is allowed for dates and partial dates, but the observed regex does not express that for date-only or partial-date forms.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative R4 status and the primitive's broad reuse increase the need for consistency between computable constraints and SHALL prose. The change is a widening rather than an R4-to-R6 rejection, but normative stability makes the reverse-exchange and validator-disagreement risk material.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 regex-valid full dateTimes without a real offset are not R4-representable, and regex-only R6 validation can disagree with R6 prose or permit semantically unsafe timestamp strings.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes, if the widening was accidental: keep the R4-style mandatory `Z` or complete numeric UTC offset for full date-times while updating wording from time zone to UTC offset. If R6 intentionally wants local full dateTimes or offsets on partial dates, the base design should state that goal explicitly and adjust the regex coherently; that choice has real R6-to-R4 migration tradeoffs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high-impact runtime and R6-to-R4 risk assessment, but disagree that a less-breaking design is simply not applicable; preserving the mandatory complete offset is a plausible lower-risk base R6 design even though this is not an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 break.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, status, and abstract flag remain stable. The baseDefinition changed from `Element` to `PrimitiveType`, but that is treated as an inherited/global primitive hierarchy change rather than a local dateTime finding.
The local snapshot still contains `dateTime`, `dateTime.id`, `dateTime.extension`, and `dateTime.value`; no local element was added, removed, renamed, split, or moved.
All compared dateTime elements retain the same cardinalities: root `0..*`, `id` `0..1`, `extension` `0..*`, and `value` `0..1`.
`dateTime` has no Reference-typed elements or target profile lists.

No local dateTime-specific invariant was added or removed. The `ele-1` and `ext-1` inherited/base constraints remain conceptually the same; wording/source/xpath metadata changes are inherited and out of scope. Regex extension changes are reported separately as value-constraint findings.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value is present on the compared dateTime elements.
`isModifier` remains false for the root, `id`, `extension`, and `value` elements.
`isSummary` remains false where present for the compared elements.
No local slicing change appears in the `dateTime` StructureDefinition snapshot or differential.

The primitive value and id continue to use XML attribute representation and the JSON primitive representation is not structurally changed. Lexical serialization constraints changed through the regex findings above.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds dateTime type-characteristic metadata
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds StructureDefinition extensions marking `dateTime` with characteristics such as `has-range`, `is-continuous`, and `has-length`. These are metadata additions and do not by themselves invalidate R4 instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Code generators, query engines, or model libraries that consume type-characteristic metadata may gain new behavior around ordering, range, or length support for `dateTime`. That should be reviewed as runtime behavior, not as an instance compatibility break.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 clarifies wording from time zone to UTC offset
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Replacing `time zone` with `UTC offset` is best read as a clarification of the required lexical suffix rather than a direct element-model break. The material compatibility concern is covered in the offset regex finding.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Documentation and parser error messages should use `UTC offset` terminology and should avoid conflating an offset such as `+02:00` with a named time zone.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 introduces `PrimitiveType` as the baseDefinition for `dateTime` and other primitives. The compatibility impact of this global hierarchy change belongs in the PrimitiveType/DataType infrastructure analysis.
Inherited `ele-1` wording and xpath/source metadata changes appear on dateTime but are base Element concerns.
